ety.text: From a- + head. Perhaps originally a nautical term, beyond the head (of a ship), then drifting into more general English usage where it is used to describe something as being in front of.

senses.d: At or towards the front; in the direction one is facing or moving.
ex: Just ahead you can see the cliffs.

senses.d: So as to be further advanced, either spatially or in an abstract sense; to be superior.
ex: He finished two laps ahead of me.
In all of his classes Jack was ahead.
There may be tough times ahead.
You've got to think ahead so as not to be unprepared.
Set the clock ahead an hour.
Push the deadline ahead a day, from the 20th to the 21st.

senses.d: At an earlier time; beforehand; in advance.

ex: Push the deadline ahead a day, from the 21st to the 20th.
[…] the Department is responding to the statutory requirement in the USA Patriot Act that moved the deadline ahead to 2003 from 2007.

grp.label: so as to be further advanced

ety.text: From de + avant. False cognate of Indonesian and Malay depan despite similarity of both words in definition and pronunciation.
Inherited from Old Spanish adelante, from delante (“in front”). Equivalent to a- + delante.

phr: have one's whole life ahead of one
